title: Visual Field Defect Mapper
summary: Pick a point on the visual pathway and predict which parts of which eye's field go dark. Then run the inference backwards from a defect to the points that could have caused it.
learningObjectives: Predict the field consequence of damage in front of, at and behind the optic chiasm.
Explain why only half the fibres crossing is what makes a field pattern informative.
Distinguish a defect confined to one eye from one that respects the vertical midline in both.
State which parts of the pathway a field pattern can identify and which it cannot.
Explain why quadrant diagrams are a teaching fiction rather than a picture of a real field examination.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. Nothing on the page examines anybody's vision and no result means anything about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native radio, checkbox and button controls throughout; the eight prediction checkboxes sit in two two-by-two grids to keep the control column short while each target keeps its full 2.75rem height. Both graphics are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables: a quadrant-by-quadrant table giving what the learner predicted and what the mapping gives for all eight cells, and a summary table of every point on the pathway. Nothing depends on colour: a lost quadrant carries a printed cross as well as a fill, a predicted quadrant carries a dot, the damage marker is a circled cross, the crossing fibres at the chiasm are dashed, and the two sides of the brain are labelled L and R. Reveals and site changes announce through the shell's polite live region. Changing a prediction after a reveal withdraws the reveal, so the marking can never be stale. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Predicting field loss from a point on the visual pathway - and finding out how little the pattern can say in reverse
simulationNotes: Idealised textbook mappings on a schematic pathway. Field quadrants are coded per eye as upper-left, lower-left, upper-right and lower-right of that eye's own field. Left optic nerve gives the whole left eye; the centre of the chiasm gives the outer half of each eye; the right optic tract, both halves of the right radiation together, and the right occipital cortex each give the left half of both fields, with the occipital case drawn with the centre spared. The right temporal radiation gives the upper-left quadrant in both eyes and the right parietal radiation the lower-left. Two of the six rows are identical in quadrant terms, which is the point of the reverse-inference challenge: four of its eight options are compatible with a complete left homonymous defect. Deliberate simplifications: quadrants are a teaching fiction, since real defects have soft edges, vary in depth rather than being present or absent, and rarely respect a quadrant boundary; real lesions are partial and produce incomplete and asymmetric defects far more often than tidy ones; macular sparing is included because every textbook includes it, and the tool states that its explanation is still argued about. The diagram is schematic, nothing is to scale, no real perimetry, image or clinical instrument is reproduced, no cause is named, and nothing on the page examines or diagnoses anybody.
